Preface. Master Ranked Blueprint Index: Sixteen Options Ranked belongs to the Library of Jerusalem blueprint shelf in the New version track, and it treats one subject only: ranking sixteen model-scale starting options so a reader can choose the most useful first build. Everything in this book is a model-scale design. It is a set of drawings, dimensions, parts and checks for a small model, not a claim that a full-scale building is complete or buildable as stated. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED. Where clear gold is named anywhere in this book, it is an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and any 2,220 km cube figure in this book is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Faith and engineering are kept distinct throughout: a faith source is cited as a faith source, and an engineering measurement is stated as a measurement, and neither is used to prove the other. In the Signature edition, Master Ranked Blueprint Index: Sixteen Options Ranked is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable. Companion catalog entries new-jerusalem-city-blueprints and new-jerusalem-geometry-scale are cross-linked by slug name in text only; this book is their book-form companion, not a rebuild of them. The model measures 640 millimetres long, 480 millimetres wide and 120 millimetres high at a drawing scale of 1:200, and the chapters that follow explain that model from its first purpose to its final handover, in an order a reader can follow with the model on the table.

Chapter 1: Overview. Chapter 1: Overview. This chapter of Master Ranked Blueprint Index: Sixteen Options Ranked deals with purpose and place, and it deals with nothing else until that subject is fully explained, because a blueprint book that mixes its subjects leaves the reader guessing at the bench. The subject of the whole book is ranking sixteen model-scale starting options so a reader can choose the most useful first build, and this chapter serves that subject directly: every number, part and check in the paragraphs below belongs to this book's model, which measures 640 millimetres by 480 millimetres by 120 millimetres at a drawing scale of 1:200. A reader who opens this chapter alone should still be able to find the model on the table, name its purpose, and follow the work to the end of the chapter without turning to another book first. In the Signature edition, Master Ranked Blueprint Index: Sixteen Options Ranked is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable.

The parts that matter for purpose and place in this book are these: rank board, rank cards, sorting rail, score ledger, option markers, foundation pad, wall panel, roof beam, fastener set. Each part is named once, measured once, and then used by that same name for the rest of the book, so that a part ordered, cut or checked under one name is never confused with a different part under a second name. The materials for this book are index board, printed rank cards, brass pins, model board, wood adhesive, clear finish. A material is chosen here for a stated reason, not for its colour alone: it must cut cleanly at model scale, hold a joint without splitting, keep its shape through a test, and accept a finish that can be inspected by eye and by touch. Where a material is named as an appearance target, as clear gold is, the book says so plainly, and the appearance target is never confused with the bulk material that would be needed at full scale, which this book does not claim to establish.

The working method for purpose and place begins with marking, not with cutting, and the book insists on that order in every chapter where a cut follows a mark. The reader first lays the model board flat, checks that it is clean and level, and marks the full length of 640 millimetres and the full width of 480 millimetres with a sharp pencil line that can be seen but not felt as a groove. Then the reader marks each part in the order the assembly chapter will follow, labels each mark with the part name from the components list, and measures every mark a second time before any saw or knife is lifted. This double marking is the cheapest test in the whole book, and it prevents the most common model failure, which is a part cut to the wrong length because a mark was trusted after a single reading. The joints used in this book are dovetail joint at the rank board; lap joint at the rank cards; pinned joint at the sorting rail; slot joint at the score ledger, and each joint is described where it is used, with the faces that meet, the fastening that holds them, and the check that proves the joint after it is made.

The numbers for this chapter come from the model's own dimensions, and they can be checked with ordinary arithmetic. The footprint of the model is 640 multiplied by 480, which is 307200 square millimetres, and the perimeter is twice the sum of length and width, which is 2240 millimetres. The height is 120 millimetres, so the simple volume figure used for ordering material is 3686400 cubic units in the book's working arithmetic, and the drawing scale of 1:200 means that one millimetre on the drawing stands for 200 millimetres on the scale drawing, a drawing convention only and not a full-scale building claim. The tolerance for joints in this book is plus or minus 0.5 millimetres, and that tolerance is applied to every joint alike: a joint that is tighter than the tolerance is accepted, a joint that is looser is reworked, and a joint that is forced into place is never accepted, because a forced joint hides a measuring error that will appear later as a gap, a twist or a crack.

The tests for this book are square check; level check; swing test; load test, and the failure modes the reader must watch for are warped panel; loose joint; misaligned leaf; blocked drain. A test is only useful if its pass mark is stated before the test is run, so each test in this book carries its own pass mark: a square check passes when both diagonals agree within the stated tolerance, a level check passes when the model sits without rocking on a flat surface, a swing test passes when a moving part moves through its full travel without binding, and a fit test passes when a part enters its place without force and leaves it without damage. When a failure mode appears, the book does not ask the reader to hide it with filler or paint. The reader stops, names the failure mode in the words used here, finds the mark or cut that caused it, corrects that mark or cut, and only then repeats the test, because a model that passes after a hidden repair teaches the wrong lesson about the design.

The tools for this book are steel ruler, craft knife, fine saw, square, clamps, and each tool is used only for the work it does well. A ruler measures and never cuts, a knife cuts and never pries, a square checks and never hammers, and clamps hold while glue sets and are removed only when the joint can stand on its own. The reader keeps the tools clean, keeps the cutting edge sharp, and keeps the work surface clear, because a cluttered bench produces the same errors as a dull blade: marks made in the wrong place, parts cut to the wrong length, and joints assembled in the wrong order. Safety in this book is simple and practical: cut away from the hands, keep fingers behind the blade, work in good light, and stop when tired, since most model errors happen at the end of a long session rather than at the start of a careful one, and a rested reader measures better than a hurried one.

In practice, a reader building Master Ranked Blueprint Index: Sixteen Options Ranked for the first time should build the smallest part first, test it, and only then build the larger parts that depend on it, because the order of building is also the order of learning in this book. The smallest part teaches the joint, the joint teaches the tolerance, the tolerance teaches the measuring habit, and the measuring habit carries through every later chapter, from materials to maintenance, without needing to be relearned. When this chapter is finished, the reader should be able to state its subject in one sentence, point to the part or measurement it concerns, and pass to the next chapter, which takes up the next subject in the same order, with the same part names, the same tolerance, and the same habit of marking twice and cutting once. That continuity is the real subject of a blueprint book: not a single clever part, but a whole model whose parts agree with each other.

Preface. The Foursquare City Frame Blueprint (model scale) belongs to the Library of Jerusalem blueprint shelf in the New version track, and it treats one subject only: a foursquare city frame in miniature, with corner posts, base rails and measure cords that set the square. Everything in this book is a model-scale design. It is a set of drawings, dimensions, parts and checks for a small model, not a claim that a full-scale building is complete or buildable as stated. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED. Where clear gold is named anywhere in this book, it is an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and any 2,220 km cube figure in this book is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Faith and engineering are kept distinct throughout: a faith source is cited as a faith source, and an engineering measurement is stated as a measurement, and neither is used to prove the other. In the Signature edition, The Foursquare City Frame Blueprint (model scale) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable. Companion catalog entries new-jerusalem-city-blueprints and new-jerusalem-geometry-scale are cross-linked by slug name in text only; this book is their book-form companion, not a rebuild of them. The model measures 383 millimetres long, 277 millimetres wide and 151 millimetres high at a drawing scale of 1:105, and the chapters that follow explain that model from its first purpose to its final handover, in an order a reader can follow with the model on the table.

Chapter 1: Overview. Chapter 1: Overview. This chapter of The Foursquare City Frame Blueprint (model scale) deals with purpose and place, and it deals with nothing else until that subject is fully explained, because a blueprint book that mixes its subjects leaves the reader guessing at the bench. The subject of the whole book is a foursquare city frame in miniature, with corner posts, base rails and measure cords that set the square, and this chapter serves that subject directly: every number, part and check in the paragraphs below belongs to this book's model, which measures 383 millimetres by 277 millimetres by 151 millimetres at a drawing scale of 1:105. A reader who opens this chapter alone should still be able to find the model on the table, name its purpose, and follow the work to the end of the chapter without turning to another book first. In the Signature edition, The Foursquare City Frame Blueprint (model scale) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable.

The parts that matter for purpose and place in this book are these: square frame, corner posts, base rails, measure cords, level markers, foundation pad, wall panel, roof beam, fastener set. Each part is named once, measured once, and then used by that same name for the rest of the book, so that a part ordered, cut or checked under one name is never confused with a different part under a second name. The materials for this book are frame timber, corner brass, measure cord, model board, wood adhesive, clear finish. A material is chosen here for a stated reason, not for its colour alone: it must cut cleanly at model scale, hold a joint without splitting, keep its shape through a test, and accept a finish that can be inspected by eye and by touch. Where a material is named as an appearance target, as clear gold is, the book says so plainly, and the appearance target is never confused with the bulk material that would be needed at full scale, which this book does not claim to establish.

The working method for purpose and place begins with marking, not with cutting, and the book insists on that order in every chapter where a cut follows a mark. The reader first lays the model board flat, checks that it is clean and level, and marks the full length of 383 millimetres and the full width of 277 millimetres with a sharp pencil line that can be seen but not felt as a groove. Then the reader marks each part in the order the assembly chapter will follow, labels each mark with the part name from the components list, and measures every mark a second time before any saw or knife is lifted. This double marking is the cheapest test in the whole book, and it prevents the most common model failure, which is a part cut to the wrong length because a mark was trusted after a single reading. The joints used in this book are lap joint at the square frame; pinned joint at the corner posts; slot joint at the base rails; braced butt joint at the measure cords, and each joint is described where it is used, with the faces that meet, the fastening that holds them, and the check that proves the joint after it is made.

The numbers for this chapter come from the model's own dimensions, and they can be checked with ordinary arithmetic. The footprint of the model is 383 multiplied by 277, which is 106091 square millimetres, and the perimeter is twice the sum of length and width, which is 1320 millimetres. The height is 151 millimetres, so the simple volume figure used for ordering material is 1601974 cubic units in the book's working arithmetic, and the drawing scale of 1:105 means that one millimetre on the drawing stands for 105 millimetres on the scale drawing, a drawing convention only and not a full-scale building claim. The tolerance for joints in this book is plus or minus 0.75 millimetres, and that tolerance is applied to every joint alike: a joint that is tighter than the tolerance is accepted, a joint that is looser is reworked, and a joint that is forced into place is never accepted, because a forced joint hides a measuring error that will appear later as a gap, a twist or a crack.

The tests for this book are level check; swing test; load test; water run test, and the failure modes the reader must watch for are loose joint; misaligned leaf; blocked drain; uneven floor. A test is only useful if its pass mark is stated before the test is run, so each test in this book carries its own pass mark: a square check passes when both diagonals agree within the stated tolerance, a level check passes when the model sits without rocking on a flat surface, a swing test passes when a moving part moves through its full travel without binding, and a fit test passes when a part enters its place without force and leaves it without damage. When a failure mode appears, the book does not ask the reader to hide it with filler or paint. The reader stops, names the failure mode in the words used here, finds the mark or cut that caused it, corrects that mark or cut, and only then repeats the test, because a model that passes after a hidden repair teaches the wrong lesson about the design.

The tools for this book are craft knife, fine saw, square, clamps, glue brush, and each tool is used only for the work it does well. A ruler measures and never cuts, a knife cuts and never pries, a square checks and never hammers, and clamps hold while glue sets and are removed only when the joint can stand on its own. The reader keeps the tools clean, keeps the cutting edge sharp, and keeps the work surface clear, because a cluttered bench produces the same errors as a dull blade: marks made in the wrong place, parts cut to the wrong length, and joints assembled in the wrong order. Safety in this book is simple and practical: cut away from the hands, keep fingers behind the blade, work in good light, and stop when tired, since most model errors happen at the end of a long session rather than at the start of a careful one, and a rested reader measures better than a hurried one.

In practice, a reader building The Foursquare City Frame Blueprint (model scale) for the first time should build the smallest part first, test it, and only then build the larger parts that depend on it, because the order of building is also the order of learning in this book. The smallest part teaches the joint, the joint teaches the tolerance, the tolerance teaches the measuring habit, and the measuring habit carries through every later chapter, from materials to maintenance, without needing to be relearned. When this chapter is finished, the reader should be able to state its subject in one sentence, point to the part or measurement it concerns, and pass to the next chapter, which takes up the next subject in the same order, with the same part names, the same tolerance, and the same habit of marking twice and cutting once. That continuity is the real subject of a blueprint book: not a single clever part, but a whole model whose parts agree with each other.

Preface. The Twelve-Gate Wall Blueprint (model scale) belongs to the Library of Jerusalem blueprint shelf in the New version track, and it treats one subject only: a twelve-gate wall in miniature, with wall panels, twelve gate markers and corner towers. Everything in this book is a model-scale design. It is a set of drawings, dimensions, parts and checks for a small model, not a claim that a full-scale building is complete or buildable as stated. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED. Where clear gold is named anywhere in this book, it is an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and any 2,220 km cube figure in this book is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Faith and engineering are kept distinct throughout: a faith source is cited as a faith source, and an engineering measurement is stated as a measurement, and neither is used to prove the other. In the Signature edition, The Twelve-Gate Wall Blueprint (model scale) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable. Companion catalog entries new-jerusalem-city-blueprints and new-jerusalem-geometry-scale are cross-linked by slug name in text only; this book is their book-form companion, not a rebuild of them. The model measures 406 millimetres long, 294 millimetres wide and 162 millimetres high at a drawing scale of 1:110, and the chapters that follow explain that model from its first purpose to its final handover, in an order a reader can follow with the model on the table.

Chapter 1: Overview. Chapter 1: Overview. This chapter of The Twelve-Gate Wall Blueprint (model scale) deals with purpose and place, and it deals with nothing else until that subject is fully explained, because a blueprint book that mixes its subjects leaves the reader guessing at the bench. The subject of the whole book is a twelve-gate wall in miniature, with wall panels, twelve gate markers and corner towers, and this chapter serves that subject directly: every number, part and check in the paragraphs below belongs to this book's model, which measures 406 millimetres by 294 millimetres by 162 millimetres at a drawing scale of 1:110. A reader who opens this chapter alone should still be able to find the model on the table, name its purpose, and follow the work to the end of the chapter without turning to another book first. In the Signature edition, The Twelve-Gate Wall Blueprint (model scale) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable.

The parts that matter for purpose and place in this book are these: wall panels, twelve gate markers, corner towers, wall walkway, wall footing, foundation pad, wall panel, roof beam, fastener set. Each part is named once, measured once, and then used by that same name for the rest of the book, so that a part ordered, cut or checked under one name is never confused with a different part under a second name. The materials for this book are wall stone, gate markers, tower timber, model board, wood adhesive, clear finish. A material is chosen here for a stated reason, not for its colour alone: it must cut cleanly at model scale, hold a joint without splitting, keep its shape through a test, and accept a finish that can be inspected by eye and by touch. Where a material is named as an appearance target, as clear gold is, the book says so plainly, and the appearance target is never confused with the bulk material that would be needed at full scale, which this book does not claim to establish.

The working method for purpose and place begins with marking, not with cutting, and the book insists on that order in every chapter where a cut follows a mark. The reader first lays the model board flat, checks that it is clean and level, and marks the full length of 406 millimetres and the full width of 294 millimetres with a sharp pencil line that can be seen but not felt as a groove. Then the reader marks each part in the order the assembly chapter will follow, labels each mark with the part name from the components list, and measures every mark a second time before any saw or knife is lifted. This double marking is the cheapest test in the whole book, and it prevents the most common model failure, which is a part cut to the wrong length because a mark was trusted after a single reading. The joints used in this book are pinned joint at the wall panels; slot joint at the twelve gate markers; braced butt joint at the corner towers; tongue-and-groove joint at the wall walkway, and each joint is described where it is used, with the faces that meet, the fastening that holds them, and the check that proves the joint after it is made.

The numbers for this chapter come from the model's own dimensions, and they can be checked with ordinary arithmetic. The footprint of the model is 406 multiplied by 294, which is 119364 square millimetres, and the perimeter is twice the sum of length and width, which is 1400 millimetres. The height is 162 millimetres, so the simple volume figure used for ordering material is 1933696 cubic units in the book's working arithmetic, and the drawing scale of 1:110 means that one millimetre on the drawing stands for 110 millimetres on the scale drawing, a drawing convention only and not a full-scale building claim. The tolerance for joints in this book is plus or minus 1.0 millimetres, and that tolerance is applied to every joint alike: a joint that is tighter than the tolerance is accepted, a joint that is looser is reworked, and a joint that is forced into place is never accepted, because a forced joint hides a measuring error that will appear later as a gap, a twist or a crack.

The tests for this book are swing test; load test; water run test; fit test, and the failure modes the reader must watch for are misaligned leaf; blocked drain; uneven floor; cracked finish. A test is only useful if its pass mark is stated before the test is run, so each test in this book carries its own pass mark: a square check passes when both diagonals agree within the stated tolerance, a level check passes when the model sits without rocking on a flat surface, a swing test passes when a moving part moves through its full travel without binding, and a fit test passes when a part enters its place without force and leaves it without damage. When a failure mode appears, the book does not ask the reader to hide it with filler or paint. The reader stops, names the failure mode in the words used here, finds the mark or cut that caused it, corrects that mark or cut, and only then repeats the test, because a model that passes after a hidden repair teaches the wrong lesson about the design.

The tools for this book are fine saw, square, clamps, glue brush, sandpaper set, and each tool is used only for the work it does well. A ruler measures and never cuts, a knife cuts and never pries, a square checks and never hammers, and clamps hold while glue sets and are removed only when the joint can stand on its own. The reader keeps the tools clean, keeps the cutting edge sharp, and keeps the work surface clear, because a cluttered bench produces the same errors as a dull blade: marks made in the wrong place, parts cut to the wrong length, and joints assembled in the wrong order. Safety in this book is simple and practical: cut away from the hands, keep fingers behind the blade, work in good light, and stop when tired, since most model errors happen at the end of a long session rather than at the start of a careful one, and a rested reader measures better than a hurried one.

In practice, a reader building The Twelve-Gate Wall Blueprint (model scale) for the first time should build the smallest part first, test it, and only then build the larger parts that depend on it, because the order of building is also the order of learning in this book. The smallest part teaches the joint, the joint teaches the tolerance, the tolerance teaches the measuring habit, and the measuring habit carries through every later chapter, from materials to maintenance, without needing to be relearned. When this chapter is finished, the reader should be able to state its subject in one sentence, point to the part or measurement it concerns, and pass to the next chapter, which takes up the next subject in the same order, with the same part names, the same tolerance, and the same habit of marking twice and cutting once. That continuity is the real subject of a blueprint book: not a single clever part, but a whole model whose parts agree with each other.

Preface. The Pearl Gate Blueprint (model scale) belongs to the Library of Jerusalem blueprint shelf in the New version track, and it treats one subject only: a pearl gate in miniature, with a single panel, a pivot and an arch. Everything in this book is a model-scale design. It is a set of drawings, dimensions, parts and checks for a small model, not a claim that a full-scale building is complete or buildable as stated. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED. Where clear gold is named anywhere in this book, it is an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and any 2,220 km cube figure in this book is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Faith and engineering are kept distinct throughout: a faith source is cited as a faith source, and an engineering measurement is stated as a measurement, and neither is used to prove the other. In the Signature edition, The Pearl Gate Blueprint (model scale) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable. Companion catalog entries new-jerusalem-city-blueprints and new-jerusalem-geometry-scale are cross-linked by slug name in text only; this book is their book-form companion, not a rebuild of them. The model measures 429 millimetres long, 311 millimetres wide and 173 millimetres high at a drawing scale of 1:115, and the chapters that follow explain that model from its first purpose to its final handover, in an order a reader can follow with the model on the table.

Chapter 1: Overview. Chapter 1: Overview. This chapter of The Pearl Gate Blueprint (model scale) deals with purpose and place, and it deals with nothing else until that subject is fully explained, because a blueprint book that mixes its subjects leaves the reader guessing at the bench. The subject of the whole book is a pearl gate in miniature, with a single panel, a pivot and an arch, and this chapter serves that subject directly: every number, part and check in the paragraphs below belongs to this book's model, which measures 429 millimetres by 311 millimetres by 173 millimetres at a drawing scale of 1:115. A reader who opens this chapter alone should still be able to find the model on the table, name its purpose, and follow the work to the end of the chapter without turning to another book first. In the Signature edition, The Pearl Gate Blueprint (model scale) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable.

The parts that matter for purpose and place in this book are these: gate panel, gate pivot, gate arch, inlay panels, gate threshold, foundation pad, wall panel, roof beam, fastener set. Each part is named once, measured once, and then used by that same name for the rest of the book, so that a part ordered, cut or checked under one name is never confused with a different part under a second name. The materials for this book are gate panel, pivot brass, inlay board, model board, wood adhesive, clear finish. A material is chosen here for a stated reason, not for its colour alone: it must cut cleanly at model scale, hold a joint without splitting, keep its shape through a test, and accept a finish that can be inspected by eye and by touch. Where a material is named as an appearance target, as clear gold is, the book says so plainly, and the appearance target is never confused with the bulk material that would be needed at full scale, which this book does not claim to establish.

The working method for purpose and place begins with marking, not with cutting, and the book insists on that order in every chapter where a cut follows a mark. The reader first lays the model board flat, checks that it is clean and level, and marks the full length of 429 millimetres and the full width of 311 millimetres with a sharp pencil line that can be seen but not felt as a groove. Then the reader marks each part in the order the assembly chapter will follow, labels each mark with the part name from the components list, and measures every mark a second time before any saw or knife is lifted. This double marking is the cheapest test in the whole book, and it prevents the most common model failure, which is a part cut to the wrong length because a mark was trusted after a single reading. The joints used in this book are slot joint at the gate panel; braced butt joint at the gate pivot; tongue-and-groove joint at the gate arch; dovetail joint at the inlay panels, and each joint is described where it is used, with the faces that meet, the fastening that holds them, and the check that proves the joint after it is made.

The numbers for this chapter come from the model's own dimensions, and they can be checked with ordinary arithmetic. The footprint of the model is 429 multiplied by 311, which is 133419 square millimetres, and the perimeter is twice the sum of length and width, which is 1480 millimetres. The height is 173 millimetres, so the simple volume figure used for ordering material is 2308148 cubic units in the book's working arithmetic, and the drawing scale of 1:115 means that one millimetre on the drawing stands for 115 millimetres on the scale drawing, a drawing convention only and not a full-scale building claim. The tolerance for joints in this book is plus or minus 0.5 millimetres, and that tolerance is applied to every joint alike: a joint that is tighter than the tolerance is accepted, a joint that is looser is reworked, and a joint that is forced into place is never accepted, because a forced joint hides a measuring error that will appear later as a gap, a twist or a crack.

The tests for this book are load test; water run test; fit test; count check, and the failure modes the reader must watch for are blocked drain; uneven floor; cracked finish; warped panel. A test is only useful if its pass mark is stated before the test is run, so each test in this book carries its own pass mark: a square check passes when both diagonals agree within the stated tolerance, a level check passes when the model sits without rocking on a flat surface, a swing test passes when a moving part moves through its full travel without binding, and a fit test passes when a part enters its place without force and leaves it without damage. When a failure mode appears, the book does not ask the reader to hide it with filler or paint. The reader stops, names the failure mode in the words used here, finds the mark or cut that caused it, corrects that mark or cut, and only then repeats the test, because a model that passes after a hidden repair teaches the wrong lesson about the design.

The tools for this book are square, clamps, glue brush, sandpaper set, marking gauge, and each tool is used only for the work it does well. A ruler measures and never cuts, a knife cuts and never pries, a square checks and never hammers, and clamps hold while glue sets and are removed only when the joint can stand on its own. The reader keeps the tools clean, keeps the cutting edge sharp, and keeps the work surface clear, because a cluttered bench produces the same errors as a dull blade: marks made in the wrong place, parts cut to the wrong length, and joints assembled in the wrong order. Safety in this book is simple and practical: cut away from the hands, keep fingers behind the blade, work in good light, and stop when tired, since most model errors happen at the end of a long session rather than at the start of a careful one, and a rested reader measures better than a hurried one.

In practice, a reader building The Pearl Gate Blueprint (model scale) for the first time should build the smallest part first, test it, and only then build the larger parts that depend on it, because the order of building is also the order of learning in this book. The smallest part teaches the joint, the joint teaches the tolerance, the tolerance teaches the measuring habit, and the measuring habit carries through every later chapter, from materials to maintenance, without needing to be relearned. When this chapter is finished, the reader should be able to state its subject in one sentence, point to the part or measurement it concerns, and pass to the next chapter, which takes up the next subject in the same order, with the same part names, the same tolerance, and the same habit of marking twice and cutting once. That continuity is the real subject of a blueprint book: not a single clever part, but a whole model whose parts agree with each other.

Preface. The Foundation Course Blueprint (twelve stones) belongs to the Library of Jerusalem blueprint shelf in the New version track, and it treats one subject only: a foundation course in miniature, with twelve stone blocks laid in a cited order. Everything in this book is a model-scale design. It is a set of drawings, dimensions, parts and checks for a small model, not a claim that a full-scale building is complete or buildable as stated. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED. Where clear gold is named anywhere in this book, it is an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and any 2,220 km cube figure in this book is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Faith and engineering are kept distinct throughout: a faith source is cited as a faith source, and an engineering measurement is stated as a measurement, and neither is used to prove the other. In the Signature edition, The Foundation Course Blueprint (twelve stones) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable. Companion catalog entries new-jerusalem-city-blueprints and new-jerusalem-geometry-scale are cross-linked by slug name in text only; this book is their book-form companion, not a rebuild of them. The model measures 452 millimetres long, 328 millimetres wide and 184 millimetres high at a drawing scale of 1:120, and the chapters that follow explain that model from its first purpose to its final handover, in an order a reader can follow with the model on the table.

Chapter 1: Overview. Chapter 1: Overview. This chapter of The Foundation Course Blueprint (twelve stones) deals with purpose and place, and it deals with nothing else until that subject is fully explained, because a blueprint book that mixes its subjects leaves the reader guessing at the bench. The subject of the whole book is a foundation course in miniature, with twelve stone blocks laid in a cited order, and this chapter serves that subject directly: every number, part and check in the paragraphs below belongs to this book's model, which measures 452 millimetres by 328 millimetres by 184 millimetres at a drawing scale of 1:120. A reader who opens this chapter alone should still be able to find the model on the table, name its purpose, and follow the work to the end of the chapter without turning to another book first. In the Signature edition, The Foundation Course Blueprint (twelve stones) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable.

The parts that matter for purpose and place in this book are these: twelve stone blocks, course rail, order markers, course bedding, level line, foundation pad, wall panel, roof beam, fastener set. Each part is named once, measured once, and then used by that same name for the rest of the book, so that a part ordered, cut or checked under one name is never confused with a different part under a second name. The materials for this book are stone blocks, course rail, bedding sand, model board, wood adhesive, clear finish. A material is chosen here for a stated reason, not for its colour alone: it must cut cleanly at model scale, hold a joint without splitting, keep its shape through a test, and accept a finish that can be inspected by eye and by touch. Where a material is named as an appearance target, as clear gold is, the book says so plainly, and the appearance target is never confused with the bulk material that would be needed at full scale, which this book does not claim to establish.

The working method for purpose and place begins with marking, not with cutting, and the book insists on that order in every chapter where a cut follows a mark. The reader first lays the model board flat, checks that it is clean and level, and marks the full length of 452 millimetres and the full width of 328 millimetres with a sharp pencil line that can be seen but not felt as a groove. Then the reader marks each part in the order the assembly chapter will follow, labels each mark with the part name from the components list, and measures every mark a second time before any saw or knife is lifted. This double marking is the cheapest test in the whole book, and it prevents the most common model failure, which is a part cut to the wrong length because a mark was trusted after a single reading. The joints used in this book are braced butt joint at the twelve stone blocks; tongue-and-groove joint at the course rail; dovetail joint at the order markers; lap joint at the course bedding, and each joint is described where it is used, with the faces that meet, the fastening that holds them, and the check that proves the joint after it is made.

The numbers for this chapter come from the model's own dimensions, and they can be checked with ordinary arithmetic. The footprint of the model is 452 multiplied by 328, which is 148256 square millimetres, and the perimeter is twice the sum of length and width, which is 1560 millimetres. The height is 184 millimetres, so the simple volume figure used for ordering material is 2727910 cubic units in the book's working arithmetic, and the drawing scale of 1:120 means that one millimetre on the drawing stands for 120 millimetres on the scale drawing, a drawing convention only and not a full-scale building claim. The tolerance for joints in this book is plus or minus 0.75 millimetres, and that tolerance is applied to every joint alike: a joint that is tighter than the tolerance is accepted, a joint that is looser is reworked, and a joint that is forced into place is never accepted, because a forced joint hides a measuring error that will appear later as a gap, a twist or a crack.

The tests for this book are water run test; fit test; count check; square check, and the failure modes the reader must watch for are uneven floor; cracked finish; warped panel; loose joint. A test is only useful if its pass mark is stated before the test is run, so each test in this book carries its own pass mark: a square check passes when both diagonals agree within the stated tolerance, a level check passes when the model sits without rocking on a flat surface, a swing test passes when a moving part moves through its full travel without binding, and a fit test passes when a part enters its place without force and leaves it without damage. When a failure mode appears, the book does not ask the reader to hide it with filler or paint. The reader stops, names the failure mode in the words used here, finds the mark or cut that caused it, corrects that mark or cut, and only then repeats the test, because a model that passes after a hidden repair teaches the wrong lesson about the design.

The tools for this book are clamps, glue brush, sandpaper set, marking gauge, steel ruler, and each tool is used only for the work it does well. A ruler measures and never cuts, a knife cuts and never pries, a square checks and never hammers, and clamps hold while glue sets and are removed only when the joint can stand on its own. The reader keeps the tools clean, keeps the cutting edge sharp, and keeps the work surface clear, because a cluttered bench produces the same errors as a dull blade: marks made in the wrong place, parts cut to the wrong length, and joints assembled in the wrong order. Safety in this book is simple and practical: cut away from the hands, keep fingers behind the blade, work in good light, and stop when tired, since most model errors happen at the end of a long session rather than at the start of a careful one, and a rested reader measures better than a hurried one.

In practice, a reader building The Foundation Course Blueprint (twelve stones) for the first time should build the smallest part first, test it, and only then build the larger parts that depend on it, because the order of building is also the order of learning in this book. The smallest part teaches the joint, the joint teaches the tolerance, the tolerance teaches the measuring habit, and the measuring habit carries through every later chapter, from materials to maintenance, without needing to be relearned. When this chapter is finished, the reader should be able to state its subject in one sentence, point to the part or measurement it concerns, and pass to the next chapter, which takes up the next subject in the same order, with the same part names, the same tolerance, and the same habit of marking twice and cutting once. That continuity is the real subject of a blueprint book: not a single clever part, but a whole model whose parts agree with each other.

Preface. The Street of Gold Blueprint (model scale) belongs to the Library of Jerusalem blueprint shelf in the New version track, and it treats one subject only: a street of gold in miniature, with a straight panel, a gold-appearance inlay and flush joints. Everything in this book is a model-scale design. It is a set of drawings, dimensions, parts and checks for a small model, not a claim that a full-scale building is complete or buildable as stated. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED. Where clear gold is named anywhere in this book, it is an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and any 2,220 km cube figure in this book is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Faith and engineering are kept distinct throughout: a faith source is cited as a faith source, and an engineering measurement is stated as a measurement, and neither is used to prove the other. In the Signature edition, The Street of Gold Blueprint (model scale) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable. Companion catalog entries new-jerusalem-city-blueprints and new-jerusalem-geometry-scale are cross-linked by slug name in text only; this book is their book-form companion, not a rebuild of them. The model measures 475 millimetres long, 345 millimetres wide and 195 millimetres high at a drawing scale of 1:125, and the chapters that follow explain that model from its first purpose to its final handover, in an order a reader can follow with the model on the table.

Chapter 1: Overview. Chapter 1: Overview. This chapter of The Street of Gold Blueprint (model scale) deals with purpose and place, and it deals with nothing else until that subject is fully explained, because a blueprint book that mixes its subjects leaves the reader guessing at the bench. The subject of the whole book is a street of gold in miniature, with a straight panel, a gold-appearance inlay and flush joints, and this chapter serves that subject directly: every number, part and check in the paragraphs below belongs to this book's model, which measures 475 millimetres by 345 millimetres by 195 millimetres at a drawing scale of 1:125. A reader who opens this chapter alone should still be able to find the model on the table, name its purpose, and follow the work to the end of the chapter without turning to another book first. In the Signature edition, The Street of Gold Blueprint (model scale) is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable.

The parts that matter for purpose and place in this book are these: street panel, gold-appearance inlay, street kerbs, street joints, finish coat, foundation pad, wall panel, roof beam, fastener set. Each part is named once, measured once, and then used by that same name for the rest of the book, so that a part ordered, cut or checked under one name is never confused with a different part under a second name. The materials for this book are street panel, inlay board, finish coat, model board, wood adhesive, clear finish. A material is chosen here for a stated reason, not for its colour alone: it must cut cleanly at model scale, hold a joint without splitting, keep its shape through a test, and accept a finish that can be inspected by eye and by touch. Where a material is named as an appearance target, as clear gold is, the book says so plainly, and the appearance target is never confused with the bulk material that would be needed at full scale, which this book does not claim to establish.

The working method for purpose and place begins with marking, not with cutting, and the book insists on that order in every chapter where a cut follows a mark. The reader first lays the model board flat, checks that it is clean and level, and marks the full length of 475 millimetres and the full width of 345 millimetres with a sharp pencil line that can be seen but not felt as a groove. Then the reader marks each part in the order the assembly chapter will follow, labels each mark with the part name from the components list, and measures every mark a second time before any saw or knife is lifted. This double marking is the cheapest test in the whole book, and it prevents the most common model failure, which is a part cut to the wrong length because a mark was trusted after a single reading. The joints used in this book are tongue-and-groove joint at the street panel; dovetail joint at the gold-appearance inlay; lap joint at the street kerbs; pinned joint at the street joints, and each joint is described where it is used, with the faces that meet, the fastening that holds them, and the check that proves the joint after it is made.

The numbers for this chapter come from the model's own dimensions, and they can be checked with ordinary arithmetic. The footprint of the model is 475 multiplied by 345, which is 163875 square millimetres, and the perimeter is twice the sum of length and width, which is 1640 millimetres. The height is 195 millimetres, so the simple volume figure used for ordering material is 3195562 cubic units in the book's working arithmetic, and the drawing scale of 1:125 means that one millimetre on the drawing stands for 125 millimetres on the scale drawing, a drawing convention only and not a full-scale building claim. The tolerance for joints in this book is plus or minus 1.0 millimetres, and that tolerance is applied to every joint alike: a joint that is tighter than the tolerance is accepted, a joint that is looser is reworked, and a joint that is forced into place is never accepted, because a forced joint hides a measuring error that will appear later as a gap, a twist or a crack.

The tests for this book are fit test; count check; square check; level check, and the failure modes the reader must watch for are cracked finish; warped panel; loose joint; misaligned leaf. A test is only useful if its pass mark is stated before the test is run, so each test in this book carries its own pass mark: a square check passes when both diagonals agree within the stated tolerance, a level check passes when the model sits without rocking on a flat surface, a swing test passes when a moving part moves through its full travel without binding, and a fit test passes when a part enters its place without force and leaves it without damage. When a failure mode appears, the book does not ask the reader to hide it with filler or paint. The reader stops, names the failure mode in the words used here, finds the mark or cut that caused it, corrects that mark or cut, and only then repeats the test, because a model that passes after a hidden repair teaches the wrong lesson about the design.

The tools for this book are glue brush, sandpaper set, marking gauge, steel ruler, craft knife, and each tool is used only for the work it does well. A ruler measures and never cuts, a knife cuts and never pries, a square checks and never hammers, and clamps hold while glue sets and are removed only when the joint can stand on its own. The reader keeps the tools clean, keeps the cutting edge sharp, and keeps the work surface clear, because a cluttered bench produces the same errors as a dull blade: marks made in the wrong place, parts cut to the wrong length, and joints assembled in the wrong order. Safety in this book is simple and practical: cut away from the hands, keep fingers behind the blade, work in good light, and stop when tired, since most model errors happen at the end of a long session rather than at the start of a careful one, and a rested reader measures better than a hurried one.

In practice, a reader building The Street of Gold Blueprint (model scale) for the first time should build the smallest part first, test it, and only then build the larger parts that depend on it, because the order of building is also the order of learning in this book. The smallest part teaches the joint, the joint teaches the tolerance, the tolerance teaches the measuring habit, and the measuring habit carries through every later chapter, from materials to maintenance, without needing to be relearned. When this chapter is finished, the reader should be able to state its subject in one sentence, point to the part or measurement it concerns, and pass to the next chapter, which takes up the next subject in the same order, with the same part names, the same tolerance, and the same habit of marking twice and cutting once. That continuity is the real subject of a blueprint book: not a single clever part, but a whole model whose parts agree with each other.

Preface. The River Channel Blueprint belongs to the Library of Jerusalem blueprint shelf in the New version track, and it treats one subject only: a river channel in miniature, with a bed, banks, fall markers and an outlet. Everything in this book is a model-scale design. It is a set of drawings, dimensions, parts and checks for a small model, not a claim that a full-scale building is complete or buildable as stated. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED. Where clear gold is named anywhere in this book, it is an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and any 2,220 km cube figure in this book is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Faith and engineering are kept distinct throughout: a faith source is cited as a faith source, and an engineering measurement is stated as a measurement, and neither is used to prove the other. In the Signature edition, The River Channel Blueprint is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable. Companion catalog entries new-jerusalem-city-blueprints and new-jerusalem-geometry-scale are cross-linked by slug name in text only; this book is their book-form companion, not a rebuild of them. The model measures 498 millimetres long, 362 millimetres wide and 206 millimetres high at a drawing scale of 1:130, and the chapters that follow explain that model from its first purpose to its final handover, in an order a reader can follow with the model on the table.

Chapter 1: Overview. Chapter 1: Overview. This chapter of The River Channel Blueprint deals with purpose and place, and it deals with nothing else until that subject is fully explained, because a blueprint book that mixes its subjects leaves the reader guessing at the bench. The subject of the whole book is a river channel in miniature, with a bed, banks, fall markers and an outlet, and this chapter serves that subject directly: every number, part and check in the paragraphs below belongs to this book's model, which measures 498 millimetres by 362 millimetres by 206 millimetres at a drawing scale of 1:130. A reader who opens this chapter alone should still be able to find the model on the table, name its purpose, and follow the work to the end of the chapter without turning to another book first. In the Signature edition, The River Channel Blueprint is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable.

The parts that matter for purpose and place in this book are these: channel bed, channel banks, fall markers, model bridges, channel outlet, foundation pad, wall panel, roof beam, fastener set. Each part is named once, measured once, and then used by that same name for the rest of the book, so that a part ordered, cut or checked under one name is never confused with a different part under a second name. The materials for this book are channel stone, bank board, fall markers, model board, wood adhesive, clear finish. A material is chosen here for a stated reason, not for its colour alone: it must cut cleanly at model scale, hold a joint without splitting, keep its shape through a test, and accept a finish that can be inspected by eye and by touch. Where a material is named as an appearance target, as clear gold is, the book says so plainly, and the appearance target is never confused with the bulk material that would be needed at full scale, which this book does not claim to establish.

The working method for purpose and place begins with marking, not with cutting, and the book insists on that order in every chapter where a cut follows a mark. The reader first lays the model board flat, checks that it is clean and level, and marks the full length of 498 millimetres and the full width of 362 millimetres with a sharp pencil line that can be seen but not felt as a groove. Then the reader marks each part in the order the assembly chapter will follow, labels each mark with the part name from the components list, and measures every mark a second time before any saw or knife is lifted. This double marking is the cheapest test in the whole book, and it prevents the most common model failure, which is a part cut to the wrong length because a mark was trusted after a single reading. The joints used in this book are dovetail joint at the channel bed; lap joint at the channel banks; pinned joint at the fall markers; slot joint at the model bridges, and each joint is described where it is used, with the faces that meet, the fastening that holds them, and the check that proves the joint after it is made.

The numbers for this chapter come from the model's own dimensions, and they can be checked with ordinary arithmetic. The footprint of the model is 498 multiplied by 362, which is 180276 square millimetres, and the perimeter is twice the sum of length and width, which is 1720 millimetres. The height is 206 millimetres, so the simple volume figure used for ordering material is 3713685 cubic units in the book's working arithmetic, and the drawing scale of 1:130 means that one millimetre on the drawing stands for 130 millimetres on the scale drawing, a drawing convention only and not a full-scale building claim. The tolerance for joints in this book is plus or minus 0.5 millimetres, and that tolerance is applied to every joint alike: a joint that is tighter than the tolerance is accepted, a joint that is looser is reworked, and a joint that is forced into place is never accepted, because a forced joint hides a measuring error that will appear later as a gap, a twist or a crack.

The tests for this book are count check; square check; level check; swing test, and the failure modes the reader must watch for are warped panel; loose joint; misaligned leaf; blocked drain. A test is only useful if its pass mark is stated before the test is run, so each test in this book carries its own pass mark: a square check passes when both diagonals agree within the stated tolerance, a level check passes when the model sits without rocking on a flat surface, a swing test passes when a moving part moves through its full travel without binding, and a fit test passes when a part enters its place without force and leaves it without damage. When a failure mode appears, the book does not ask the reader to hide it with filler or paint. The reader stops, names the failure mode in the words used here, finds the mark or cut that caused it, corrects that mark or cut, and only then repeats the test, because a model that passes after a hidden repair teaches the wrong lesson about the design.

The tools for this book are sandpaper set, marking gauge, steel ruler, craft knife, fine saw, and each tool is used only for the work it does well. A ruler measures and never cuts, a knife cuts and never pries, a square checks and never hammers, and clamps hold while glue sets and are removed only when the joint can stand on its own. The reader keeps the tools clean, keeps the cutting edge sharp, and keeps the work surface clear, because a cluttered bench produces the same errors as a dull blade: marks made in the wrong place, parts cut to the wrong length, and joints assembled in the wrong order. Safety in this book is simple and practical: cut away from the hands, keep fingers behind the blade, work in good light, and stop when tired, since most model errors happen at the end of a long session rather than at the start of a careful one, and a rested reader measures better than a hurried one.

In practice, a reader building The River Channel Blueprint for the first time should build the smallest part first, test it, and only then build the larger parts that depend on it, because the order of building is also the order of learning in this book. The smallest part teaches the joint, the joint teaches the tolerance, the tolerance teaches the measuring habit, and the measuring habit carries through every later chapter, from materials to maintenance, without needing to be relearned. When this chapter is finished, the reader should be able to state its subject in one sentence, point to the part or measurement it concerns, and pass to the next chapter, which takes up the next subject in the same order, with the same part names, the same tolerance, and the same habit of marking twice and cutting once. That continuity is the real subject of a blueprint book: not a single clever part, but a whole model whose parts agree with each other.

Chapter 1: Overview. Chapter 1: Overview. This chapter of The Tree of Life Grove Blueprint deals with purpose and place, and it deals with nothing else until that subject is fully explained, because a blueprint book that mixes its subjects leaves the reader guessing at the bench. The subject of the whole book is a tree grove in miniature, with tree models on two banks, fruit markers and paths, and this chapter serves that subject directly: every number, part and check in the paragraphs below belongs to this book's model, which measures 521 millimetres by 379 millimetres by 217 millimetres at a drawing scale of 1:135. A reader who opens this chapter alone should still be able to find the model on the table, name its purpose, and follow the work to the end of the chapter without turning to another book first. In the Signature edition, The Tree of Life Grove Blueprint is presented as a Signature original: the same measurements are stated in plain numbers so any reader can repeat the checks, and a Signature working note is added at each stage, marking where the Signature choice differs from a generic model while keeping every dimension identical and checkable.

The parts that matter for purpose and place in this book are these: tree models, fruit markers, grove banks, grove paths, grove irrigation, foundation pad, wall panel, roof beam, fastener set. Each part is named once, measured once, and then used by that same name for the rest of the book, so that a part ordered, cut or checked under one name is never confused with a different part under a second name. The materials for this book are tree timber, fruit markers, path gravel, model board, wood adhesive, clear finish. A material is chosen here for a stated reason, not for its colour alone: it must cut cleanly at model scale, hold a joint without splitting, keep its shape through a test, and accept a finish that can be inspected by eye and by touch. Where a material is named as an appearance target, as clear gold is, the book says so plainly, and the appearance target is never confused with the bulk material that would be needed at full scale, which this book does not claim to establish.

The working method for purpose and place begins with marking, not with cutting, and the book insists on that order in every chapter where a cut follows a mark. The reader first lays the model board flat, checks that it is clean and level, and marks the full length of 521 millimetres and the full width of 379 millimetres with a sharp pencil line that can be seen but not felt as a groove. Then the reader marks each part in the order the assembly chapter will follow, labels each mark with the part name from the components list, and measures every mark a second time before any saw or knife is lifted. This double marking is the cheapest test in the whole book, and it prevents the most common model failure, which is a part cut to the wrong length because a mark was trusted after a single reading. The joints used in this book are lap joint at the tree models; pinned joint at the fruit markers; slot joint at the grove banks; braced butt joint at the grove paths, and each joint is described where it is used, with the faces that meet, the fastening that holds them, and the check that proves the joint after it is made.

The numbers for this chapter come from the model's own dimensions, and they can be checked with ordinary arithmetic. The footprint of the model is 521 multiplied by 379, which is 197459 square millimetres, and the perimeter is twice the sum of length and width, which is 1800 millimetres. The height is 217 millimetres, so the simple volume figure used for ordering material is 4284860 cubic units in the book's working arithmetic, and the drawing scale of 1:135 means that one millimetre on the drawing stands for 135 millimetres on the scale drawing, a drawing convention only and not a full-scale building claim. The tolerance for joints in this book is plus or minus 0.75 millimetres, and that tolerance is applied to every joint alike: a joint that is tighter than the tolerance is accepted, a joint that is looser is reworked, and a joint that is forced into place is never accepted, because a forced joint hides a measuring error that will appear later as a gap, a twist or a crack.

The tests for this book are square check; level check; swing test; load test, and the failure modes the reader must watch for are loose joint; misaligned leaf; blocked drain; uneven floor. A test is only useful if its pass mark is stated before the test is run, so each test in this book carries its own pass mark: a square check passes when both diagonals agree within the stated tolerance, a level check passes when the model sits without rocking on a flat surface, a swing test passes when a moving part moves through its full travel without binding, and a fit test passes when a part enters its place without force and leaves it without damage. When a failure mode appears, the book does not ask the reader to hide it with filler or paint. The reader stops, names the failure mode in the words used here, finds the mark or cut that caused it, corrects that mark or cut, and only then repeats the test, because a model that passes after a hidden repair teaches the wrong lesson about the design.

The tools for this book are marking gauge, steel ruler, craft knife, fine saw, square, and each tool is used only for the work it does well. A ruler measures and never cuts, a knife cuts and never pries, a square checks and never hammers, and clamps hold while glue sets and are removed only when the joint can stand on its own. The reader keeps the tools clean, keeps the cutting edge sharp, and keeps the work surface clear, because a cluttered bench produces the same errors as a dull blade: marks made in the wrong place, parts cut to the wrong length, and joints assembled in the wrong order. Safety in this book is simple and practical: cut away from the hands, keep fingers behind the blade, work in good light, and stop when tired, since most model errors happen at the end of a long session rather than at the start of a careful one, and a rested reader measures better than a hurried one.

In practice, a reader building The Tree of Life Grove Blueprint for the first time should build the smallest part first, test it, and only then build the larger parts that depend on it, because the order of building is also the order of learning in this book. The smallest part teaches the joint, the joint teaches the tolerance, the tolerance teaches the measuring habit, and the measuring habit carries through every later chapter, from materials to maintenance, without needing to be relearned. When this chapter is finished, the reader should be able to state its subject in one sentence, point to the part or measurement it concerns, and pass to the next chapter, which takes up the next subject in the same order, with the same part names, the same tolerance, and the same habit of marking twice and cutting once. That continuity is the real subject of a blueprint book: not a single clever part, but a whole model whose parts agree with each other.
